source_refs.note: Topic 23.7.2 (PDF 114); the aromatic examples are given in the esters figure of topic 23.7.1.

blocks.text: An ester is hydrolysed slowly to a carboxylic acid and an alcohol (or a phenol); the reaction is catalysed by acid or by base. Aliphatic esters were described in topic 23.4.1. Aromatic esters are hydrolysed in the same way, giving aryl carboxylic acids and alcohols or phenol: C6H5COOC2H5 + H2O -> C6H5COOH + C2H5OH (ethyl benzoate to benzoic acid and ethanol, H+ or OH-); C6H5COOCH3 + H2O -> C6H5COOH + CH3OH (methyl benzoate to benzoic acid and methanol).

blocks.alt: Top: R-CO-OH + H-O-R' <=> R-CO-O-R' + H2O, with the OH of the acid and the H of the alcohol boxed in orange, and the ethyl propanoate example. Middle: CH3COCl + CH3CH2OH -> CH3COOCH2CH3 + HCl and C6H5COCl + C6H5OH -> C6H5COOC6H5 + HCl, which go to completion. Bottom: hydrolysis of ethyl benzoate and methyl benzoate to benzoic acid and the alcohol.
blocks.caption: Making and hydrolysing esters (original diagram after the book's equations).
blocks.long_description: In esterification the water that forms comes from the OH of the acid and the H of the alcohol. Using an acyl chloride instead of the acid gives a faster, complete reaction because HCl is lost instead of water. Hydrolysis is the reverse of esterification, splitting the ester back into the acid and the alcohol.
